edits.definition: The Peninsular Plateau is the vast, triangular tableland that forms the southern heart of India, edged by the Western and Eastern Ghats and sloping towards the east into wide river valleys. It is built of some of the oldest, hardest rocks on Earth — the same ancient crust that once formed part of the supercontinent Gondwana — so it has stood stable while the young Himalayas rose in the north. Its level-topped surface holds rich mineral belts (iron, coal, manganese), its black lava soils grow cotton, and its rivers falling over the Ghats create the waterfalls of the peninsula.

The Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro is the most famous public building of the Harappan civilization: a large rectangular tank about 12 by 7 metres, lined with tightly fitted baked bricks and sealed watertight with bitumen, with steps leading down on opposite sides and galleries and rooms ringing it. Water filled it from a large well beside it, and drained out through a corbelled vault. Its scale and care — no household shared in its construction — suggest a collective ritual bath on special occasions, and it stands as proof that Harappan engineers could plan, waterproof and drain a public monument nearly five thousand years ago.

Comparing fractions means deciding which of two of them holds more of the whole — which slice is bigger. The rule book has three pages: same denominators, compare numerators (3/7 > 2/7 — more of the same-sized slices); same numerators, the smaller denominator wins (3/5 > 3/8 — fewer slices means bigger slices); and unlike both, bring them to a common denominator by finding the LCM (2/3 vs 3/4 → 8/12 vs 9/12 → 3/4 wins). The third method settles every case, and the first two are its shortcuts.

Forming algebraic expressions is writing a number-story with letters in it: the unknown is named with a variable, the known operations are stated around it, and the relationship becomes one compact expression. 'A number increased by seven' becomes x + 7; 'five times a number less than twenty' becomes 20 − 5x; 'the cost of 3 pens at ₹p each' becomes 3p. Once written, the expression works for every possible value of the unknown — which is the whole point: one expression carries a rule that arithmetic would have to restate for each separate number.

A polygon is a simple closed figure on a flat surface, built from three or more straight line segments that meet only at their endpoints — triangles, quadrilaterals, pentagons and all their many-sided cousins. It is called regular when every side has the same length and every interior angle the same measure — the equilateral triangle, the square, the regular pentagon — and irregular when sides or angles vary. Curved or open figures are not polygons at all: straight sides and closure are the entry requirement, and the naming follows the sides (penta-, hexa-, octa-…).

A triangle is the closed figure made of three sides, and its three interior angles always add to exactly 180° — a law so fixed that any two angles hand you the third. A quadrilateral, closed by four sides, carries interior angles that always total 360° — draw one diagonal and its two triangles make the law visible, 180° + 180°. These angle sums are the workhorses of school geometry: missing angles are found by subtraction from the known total, and the same logic stretches to any polygon, where (n − 2) × 180° gives the sum for n sides.

Geometric construction is drawing with proof built in: figures made with ruler, compass (and protractor where allowed) by exact, ordered steps so that the result is accurate and anyone can repeat it. Each tool has its job — the ruler draws straight lines and measures lengths, the compass copies lengths and draws circles whose equal radii guarantee equality, the protractor reads and marks angles. Unlike freehand sketching, a construction must follow the logical sequence (draw the base, copy an angle, mark the point, join) and every arc used must remain visible — the arcs are the working, the drawing is the answer.

Materials answer one question about light: how much gets through? Transparent materials — clear glass, clean water, plain air — pass nearly all the light, so objects behind them are seen sharply. Translucent materials — frosted glass, butter paper, thin curtains — let light through but scatter it, so a glow passes while shapes blur into shadows. Opaque materials — wood, metal, brick — block light completely, casting a dark shadow and showing nothing beyond. The classification depends on what happens to the light ray: pass it, scatter it, or stop it — and the same substance can change class, as ground glass shows.

A municipality is the government of a town or city at the residents' own level: a body of elected ward councillors, led by a chairperson or mayor, that runs the daily civic life of urban areas — water supply, drainage and sewerage, garbage collection, street lighting, roads and footpaths, parks, birth and death registration, and licences for shops and markets. Larger cities have Municipal Corporations, smaller towns Municipal Councils and nagar panchayats, but the design is the same: voters elect ward representatives every five years, taxes on property and services pay the bills, and decisions about the neighbourhood are taken by people who live in it.

Double coincidence of wants is the roadblock at the heart of barter: for a direct exchange to happen, each trader must want exactly what the other offers at the same time. A farmer with wheat needs shoes, but the shoemaker wants vegetables, not wheat — two trades fail where money would complete both. Because every swap demands this lucky mutual match, barter wastes effort in endless searching, leaves no fair way to price one good against another, and splits every trade into indivisible lumps. Money dissolves the problem: sell wheat to anyone for coins, buy shoes from anyone who takes coins — the coincidence requirement disappears.

The medieval centuries remade India's cultural landscape. New regional languages took shape from people's speech — Bengali, Marathi, Tamil devotional verse, early Hindi — and carried poetry and prayer to listeners who never read Sanskrit; bhakti and Sufi movements gave religion a popular, emotional voice that questioned ritual and caste; and architecture answered with new monumental styles — temples rising in northern and southern idioms, mosques, dargahs, minarets and new towns built by successive sultanates. Sanskrit learning continued alongside, but culture now lived in many tongues and reached many more people — the medieval synthesis that made India's cultural map recognisably modern.

Numbers are the labels by which we measure and order the world: specific values standing for quantity (three notebooks), position (second in the queue) or measurement (two and a half metres). Everyday life runs on them — the clock's hours, the shop's prices, the cricket score, the bus route number, the marks on an exam. Each use belongs to a number family — counting numbers for quantity, ordinal numbers for order, decimals for measurement — and fluency with them is less about reciting than about choosing the right kind of number for the job at hand.

The balance model pictures an equation as a two-pan scale: the expression on the left and the number on the right sit in the two pans, and the equals sign is the fulcrum — the scale reads balanced because both sides hold equal weight. Solve it by doing to both pans whatever keeps them equal: adding the same weight to each, removing the same from each, doubling each, halving each. One wrong move — subtracting from only one side — tips the scale and the equation is lost. The model's lesson is the method's guarantee: equality survives only identical treatment of both sides.

A ratio compares two quantities of the same kind by division, telling how many times one contains the other: 3 pens to 5 pens is 3 : 5, read 'three is to five'. It has no units — the kind cancels — and it behaves like a fraction: 3 : 5 = 6 : 10 = 15 : 25. A proportion is the statement that two ratios are equal, written 3 : 5 : : 6 : 10; its cross-products always multiply equal (3 × 10 = 5 × 6), and this cross-check is the test for whether two given ratios truly match — the working rule behind recipes, maps and unit pricing.

A point is a location and nothing else — no length, no width, marked by a dot and named with a capital letter. A line segment is the straight shortest path joining two fixed endpoints, with a definite, measurable length; a line is the segment stretched endlessly in both directions, with no endpoints and no length to measure; a ray starts at one point and runs forever in one direction, like a beam of light. These four ideas are geometry's alphabet: every figure that follows — angle, triangle, polygon — is spelled out of points joined by segments.

Data is any collection of facts, numbers or observations gathered about a question — the marks of a class, the daily temperatures of a fortnight, the favourite fruits of a school. Raw data is just a heap until it is handled: collected with a purpose, organised (tallies and frequency tables), presented so the eye can read it (bar graphs, pictographs, double bar graphs) and interpreted for what it proves — the largest, the smallest, the trend, the comparison. Data handling is that full journey from question to organised answer, and it is how decisions get evidence instead of guesswork.

A geometric pattern is a sequence of shapes arranged by a rule — repeating (triangle, square, triangle…), growing (one square, then three, then five — adding two each time), or rotating and turning through fixed angles. Every pattern hides its rule in the count of some element: matchsticks per step, dots per row, squares per figure. Finding the rule converts seeing into predicting — the twentieth figure can be described without building nineteen — and the hunt for it is the first training in algebra's habit: look for what changes, and express it in terms of what step you are on.

The water cycle is the Sun-driven journey of water around the planet: heat evaporates water from oceans, lakes and rivers into invisible vapour; the vapour rises, cools and condenses on dust into clouds; winds carry the clouds until the drops grow heavy and fall as rain or snow; and the fallen water runs off as rivers, soaks in as groundwater, or freezes into ice — feeding plants, animals and cities before returning to the sea to begin again. Evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection are its four stations, and since the total water on Earth never changes, the glass you drink from today may once have been monsoon over the sea.

Sources of light are the objects that make light of their own, and they come in two families. Natural sources need no human hand: the Sun — the greatest of all — the stars, fireflies, glow-worms, and the rare glow of some deep-sea fish and fungi. Artificial sources are made by us: the electric bulb and tube-light, the candle and oil lamp, the torch's LED, fireworks. Light itself is a form of energy that travels out from these sources and makes vision possible; objects that do not produce it — the moon, a book, this page — are only visible because they reflect some other source's light into our eyes.

Photosynthesis is the food-making process of green plants: in the leaves, the green pigment chlorophyll traps sunlight and uses its energy to combine water from the soil with carbon dioxide from the air, producing glucose (the plant's food) and releasing oxygen into the air as a by-product. The word equation reads: carbon dioxide + water — sunlight and chlorophyll → glucose + oxygen. It is the single bridge between the Sun's energy and all life on Earth, because plants store that captured energy as food which every animal — directly or indirectly — ends up eating.
